caption:
Microsoft offered voluntary exit packages to about 60,000 employees in October.
Asked on a podcast if layoffs could follow, Satya Nadella said: "I wish I could just sit here and say it'll all be the same. I cannot."
Microsoft says the offer is not a layoff.

site_article.headline: Nadella says he cannot promise Microsoft jobs will stay the same after 60,000 exit offers
site_article.dek: The Microsoft chief executive linked the voluntary exit offer to how AI is changing software work, while the company says the package is not a layoff.
site_article.summary: Microsoft chief executive Satya Nadella told The Pragmatic Engineer podcast that he could not promise work at the company would stay the same, after Microsoft offered voluntary exit packages to about 60,000 employees in October. Microsoft has said it expects fewer than 5% of eligible staff to accept.
site_article.seo_title: Nadella on Microsoft's 60,000 exit offers and AI jobs
site_article.seo_description: Satya Nadella says he cannot promise Microsoft jobs will stay the same after 60,000 employees got voluntary exit offers. What he said and what the offer covers.
site_article.answer_summary: Microsoft's voluntary exit offer is open to about 60,000 employees, and Nadella said he could not promise that work would stay the same, though the company says the offer is not a layoff.
site_article.hero_alt: Portrait photo of Microsoft chief executive Satya Nadella.

paragraphs.text: Microsoft chief executive Satya Nadella said he could not promise employees that their work would stay the same, in an interview with former Microsoft engineer Gergely Orosz on The Pragmatic Engineer podcast, Windows Latest reported on November 19, 2026. Orosz asked him directly whether the company's recent voluntary exit offers could come before layoffs.

Nadella answered that he wished he could say everything would remain as it is, but that he could not, according to Windows Latest. He said the company's workforce of more than 200,000 people will have to be organized in different ways as AI changes how software is built, and that the opportunity ahead may look different in team sizes and team workflows.

Microsoft introduced the Voluntary Exit Offer on October 26, 2026, in a post by chief people officer Amy Coleman. Windows Latest reported that it is open to employees at level 70 and below, the level just under vice president, in participating teams in the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom and India, and that it comes with financial support. Unlike a voluntary retirement program Microsoft ran in April for US staff, it has no age or tenure requirement.

About 60,000 employees are eligible. A Microsoft spokesperson told Fortune that the company expects fewer than 5% to accept, which would mean fewer than 3,000 departures, according to Windows Latest. The outlet has described the package as close to standard severance. Microsoft has said the offer is not a layoff and that AI is not the reason for it.

In the podcast, Nadella said he would not want to be stuck in a team that has not transformed, even inside Microsoft, and admitted that not every part of the company has fully taken in the change. He told employees in that position that they could leave, then said he did not want them to, because there are plenty of other teams inside Microsoft, Windows Latest reported.

Nadella also said that with code generation now cheap, the hard part has become verification, and named the forward deployed engineer as one of the fastest growing roles. On hiring of junior staff, he said the first step is moving existing employees into places that make sense, followed by college hires, according to the same report.

At the DealBook Summit on November 18, Nadella described the team behind Cowork, Microsoft's AI agent inside its Microsoft 365 apps, as 11 developers working with AI who build a software factory that in turn builds the product, TokenPost reported. He said he expects employees in other fields to direct AI agents rather than complete every task themselves, and that the exit offer was meant to give employees a say in decisions about their futures.

The comments follow a June interview with LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman, resurfaced on X in early November, in which Nadella described a thought experiment of Microsoft's employees working in a loop with 2 million or 20 million AI agents, according to Windows Latest. Microsoft also cut about 4,800 roles in July, the outlet reported.

Microsoft is presenting the offer as a choice rather than a cut, and the expected uptake is small relative to a workforce of more than 200,000. Nadella's answer is notable because he declined to give employees the reassurance the question invited, and tied the change directly to how AI is reshaping the way teams build software.

The number of employees who actually accept the offer, and whether Microsoft announces further job cuts afterward, will show whether the voluntary route is enough for the restructuring Nadella describes.
